To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) social contacts of older Europeans are positively associated with welfare spending on care for older people and health services, and negatively associated with income inequality, (2) the association of social contacts with income inequality and welfare spending is not the same for all age groups.

income inequality and old-age income poverty reduce the likelihood that older people have a close contact, and that the negative effects of income inequality and old age poverty on social contacts can be mitigated by high levels of welfare spending on health and care for older people.
the amount of social contact of older people in Europe is associated with welfare spending, especially on care for older people and health, and income inequality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the social context of older people and its consequences for health.
the question of whether and to what extent social contacts of older persons can be improved through social policies.
the social contacts of older Europeans, and how these contacts are related to the social and political context.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of income inequality and welfare spending on the social contacts of older persons are not very pronounced, but they do have some impact.
income inequality and welfare spending are both important factors in explaining cross-national differences in social contacts of older Europeans.
social contacts are a complex phenomenon and that there is no simple relationship between welfare spending, income inequality and social contacts of older persons.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
social contacts of older persons can be increased by welfare spending and by reducing economic inequality.
the amount of social ties of older people is not a simple function of income inequality and welfare spending, but rather a complex outcome of the interplay between these factors.
social contacts of older Europeans are not only influenced by individual resources but also by the welfare state.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the amount of social contact of older people is not only a matter of individual preferences but also depends on the social and economic context.
social contacts of older persons are not only a private matter.
the social contact network of older people can be strengthened by policies and programs that reduce income inequality, poverty and old-age dependency.
